items.title: Morning Briefing: Nov. 21, 2026
items.excerpt: Here's a rundown of all the news you need to know for Saturday, including US President Donald Trump threatening military action against Iran for a rumored "dirty bomb" plot targeting Washington and downplaying a wave of US outages, Denmark expelling the Russian defense attache and halting non-essential visas for Russian citizens, and German Chancellor Friedrich Merz calling for a "360-degree partnership" with Qatar. US President Donald Trump threatened military action against Iran for a rumored "dirty bomb" plot targeting Washington, saying: "If they do (that), we’re going to fight." He insisted his administration is closely monitoring Tehran and had extensive intelligence on its activities. "We will not allow that." Speaking at his first news conference since returning from Asia, Trump also downplayed a wave of banking, technology, and service outages across the country, attributing many to companies upgrading their systems and saying "they’re all separate events." He blamed air traffic control disruptions on infrastructure that is "55 years old and older" and said his administration is seeking $50 billion from Congress to build a new system. Asked about firing National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross, Trump said: “Because I didn’t think that person was good enough.” - Denmark expels Russian defense attache, halts non-essential visas for Russians Denmark has ordered the Russian defense attache to leave within seven days and will halt all non-essential visas for Russian citizens, according to Foreign Minister Lars Lokke Rasmussen. He called the expulsion a strong signal to Moscow, adding "enough is enough," and said Denmark is continuing to support Ukraine. Rasmussen said the government plans to lift the obligation to receive ships linked to Russia and would discuss visa restrictions with other Schengen countries, singling out France, while Denmark will not expel all Russian diplomats as it needs to maintain communication with Moscow. Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen said Danish authorities linked a foiled assassination plot targeting a US-Ukrainian citizen on Danish soil to Russian intelligence services, allegedly involving individuals tied to the banned Loyal to Familia gang. - Germany's Merz hails strategic ties with Qatar, seeks '360-degree partnership' German Chancellor Friedrich Merz called for a "360-degree partnership" with Qatar, welcoming its pledge to invest an additional €15 billion ($16.5 billion) in Germany and praising its efforts to end the war between the US and Iran. "Qatar is doing an incredibly valuable job as a mediator between the parties to the conflict," he told a news conference in Berlin with Qatari Emir Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani. Merz said the leaders agreed to expand cooperation in the economy, energy, defense, and security, and that Syria’s reconstruction remains a shared priority, with the investment expected to strengthen areas such as artificial intelligence, semiconductors, and aviation. Germany and Qatar signed two agreements to strengthen security and defense cooperation. Sheikh Tamim described Germany as an important partner and urged de-escalation, the protection of civilians and unhindered humanitarian assistance, saying “lasting peace is only possible with genuine political solutions.”

The president did not provide details in his Friday briefing with reporters and said he hadn’t yet told his own officials about his plan. His position highlights a divide between a president who views expansion of data centers as critical to winning the AI race and an American public that is deeply skeptical of their benefits. The Republican president urged Americans to welcome their construction and extract concessions from the tech companies seeking to build them. The midterms ushered in a wave of Democrats pledging to clamp down on the energy-hungry data centers.

items.title: US recession gauges show no alarms on Nov. 20, St. Louis Fed says | EconoTimes
items.excerpt: All four standard U.S. recession gauges remained below their alarm thresholds on Nov. 20, leaving no recession signal, the St. Louis Fed and Labor Department said. The 10-year Treasury yield exceeded the two-year yield by 0.29 percentage point, keeping the yield curve out of inversion. It had been inverted for zero days over the past two years. The Sahm rule stood at 0.00, below its 0.5 recession threshold. The rule compares the three-month average unemployment rate with its lowest three-month average over the previous year. The U.S. unemployment rate was 4.1%, unchanged from its one-year low, the Labor Department said. The gauge has a threshold of 0.0 percentage point above that low in the supplied measure. The four-week average of initial jobless claims was 198,000, up 1.3% from its one-year low, according to the Labor Department. The claims gauge also remained below its recession threshold. items.title: Fed's Cook says inflation has been above target for 67 months and defends her call for a second rise | FinanceInTime
items.excerpt: Published Nov 21, 2026, 01:11 UTC 3 min read ... ## Key points - Cook said inflation, measured by PCE prices, has been above the Fed's 2% target for 67 months. - The 12-month PCE change was an estimated 3.8% in October, and core PCE was 3.2%. - She dissented in October, preferring a quarter-point increase from the 3.75%-4% range. - Her reasons: financial conditions too accommodative, and a risk of falling behind the curve. - Third-quarter GDP rose at a 3.4% annual pace and unemployment was 4.1% in October. Federal Reserve Governor Lisa D. Cook said on Friday that inflation has exceeded the Fed's 2% target for 67 months and that she wanted a second rate increase in October, according to the text of her speech at a Central Bank of Chile conference in Santiago. ## A dissent explained in two reasons Cook spoke at the 29th annual conference of the Central Bank of Chile. She said the views were her own and not necessarily those of her colleagues on the Fed Board or the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC). The FOMC raised the target range for the federal funds rate in September to 3.75%-4%, Cook said. At its October meeting, the committee voted to hold the rate steady. She dissented and preferred a further quarter-point increase. She gave two reasons. The first was that financial conditions are "too accommodative" while inflation is above target. Cook said the current stance of policy "does not appear to be curtailing the AI buildout" and that equity prices continue to support consumer spending. The second was urgency: waiting longer, she said, "risks getting behind the curve," and if that happens, "additional and larger rate increases may be required later to catch up." Cook said she is skeptical that September's single quarter-point increase will be enough to change the path of inflation. She added that the number and size of future adjustments should be informed by how the economy reacts to the Fed's actions. ## Inflation at 3.8% and a broad list of prices Based on data released the previous week, Cook said, the 12-month change in the personal consumption expenditures (PCE) price index was estimated at 3.8% in October. Core PCE, which excludes food and energy, was 3.2%. She said the most recent release showed prices rising briskly in a very broad range of categories, including airfare, appliances, furniture, hotels and restaurants. That point matters to her argument that energy is not the only source of pressure: the core measure, she said, "underscores that, while energy is a significant contributor to inflation, the sources of price pressure facing American families are increasingly varied." ## Growth and jobs give her little reason to wait Cook described an economy that is accelerating. GDP rose at a 3.4% annual pace in the third quarter, and real household spending rose at an annualized 3.8%. The unemployment rate was 4.1% in October, and payrolls climbed by 165,000. She tied part of the acceleration to the AI infrastructure buildout. Companies have announced plans for more than $2 trillion in specific data center construction projects in the US, Cook said, and only a fraction of that has been realized so far. By some estimates, roughly half of the world's data-center capacity under construction is outside the US.

items.title: GMT EIGHT - Latest - Fed Chair Warsh gives no signal on October rate move
items.excerpt: Fed Chair Kevin Warsh did not endorse or push back on recent signals from colleagues that officials aren't in a hurry to raise interest rates this month. Warsh said the Fed no longer gives advance guidance on policy decisions. "I'm not going to prejudge the meeting. I'm not going to say that I'm likely to do whatever at the coming meeting," Warsh said. "The Fed is turning a new page, and we just don't do that anymore." Warsh made the remarks Friday morning local time during a moderated conversation on the sidelines of the International Monetary Fund meetings in Bangkok. It came as Fed officials were about to enter their quiet period ahead of their Oct. 27-28 meeting. ... Two weeks ago, however, senior officials who consult with Warsh on policy strategy signaled the Fed wasn't in a hurry to raise rates again this month. Soon after, the probability of an October rate rise implied by futures markets fell sharply. This week, however, the September inflation data came in firmer than expected. Core consumer prices, which exclude volatile food and energy items, rose 0.33% in September from the prior month, the second straight strong monthly gain. A separate measure of producer prices released Thursday was also strong.

items.title: Democrat-controlled Congress faces task of reforming Trump’s immigration agenda | U.S. | EL PAÍS English
items.excerpt: After the economy, the aggressive immigration policy implemented by the administration of Donald Trump was the main reason U.S. voters punished the Republican Party and gave the Democrats a historic victory in the midterms. The Democratic Party will hold a majority in the United States Congress starting January 3. In the House of Representatives it will occupy at least 256 of the 435 seats after taking 42 seats from the Republicans. In the Senate it will hold 55 seats, eight more than before. The victors face the arduous task of changing an immigration system widely regarded as broken and that Congress has been unable to reform for decades. Amid Democratic euphoria over the win, ending Trump’s anti-immigrant crusade has emerged as one of their legislative priorities. Whether they succeed will not depend solely on them. A Democrat-controlled Congress will coincide with the last two years of Trump’s term. The president, as is typical for him, has sent mixed signals about how he wants to address immigration. Just a week ago he admitted in an interview on CBS’s 60 Minutes that his immigration policy had been too harsh and that people who were taxpaying workers had been deported. Hours after the interview was recorded, however, he promoted the architect of the administration’s most hardline immigration stance, Stephen Miller, to White House chief of staff. In later remarks, Trump clarified that there would be no amnesty and that his policy had not changed. ... But the reality is that the landscape has changed with the Democrats taking control of Congress. Markwayne Mullin, secretary of the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), said Trump encouraged him to work with the Democrats on immigration reform after telling him he had received many calls about the issue. ... Among the immigration bills that have so far failed in the House of Representatives, one stands a better chance of succeeding: the Dream Act, a bill that grants legal residency and opens a path to citizenship for foreigners who arrived undocumented as children. Many are beneficiaries of the DACA program (Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals) and have grown up, studied, worked and formed families in the only country they consider home. Trump has tried to end the program, created under the Barack Obama administration, during his two terms, but courts have blocked him. The so-called “dreamers” are the migrants with the broadest support across the political spectrum. The bill needs only one more Republican representative’s signature to be brought to the floor of the House. “My American Dream and Promise discharge petition has 217 signatures. 214 Democrats and three Republicans. We just need one more Republican signature to get it to the finish line and force a vote. ... In addition to the Dream Act, there is another legislative proposal with broad bipartisan support: the Dignity Act, which provides for the legalization of ... Even if the bills pass both chambers, uncertainty remains over whether Trump — who has the power to veto them — will sign them.

items.title: House unconstitutionally passed spending bill in 2022, court rules
items.excerpt: 20, 2026, 9:30 PM EST / Source: Reuters ... The House of Representatives unconstitutionally passed a $1.7 trillion government funding bill in 2022 through a pandemic-era rule allowing lawmakers to vote by proxy rather than in person, a federal appeals court ruled on Friday. The New Orleans-based 5th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals voted 9-8 to uphold an injunction that outgoing Republican Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton secured blocking enforcement of a provision of that measure that gave pregnant workers stronger legal protections. Democrat Nancy Pelosi, the speaker of the House at the time, helped implement the proxy voting rule in May 2020 following the onset of the Covid-19 pandemic as an emergency measure. The rule was ditched when Republicans took control of the House after the November 2022 elections. Before Republicans took control, the House used the proxy voting rule to pass a spending package that included the provision Paxton challenged, called the Pregnant Workers Fairness Act. It was signed into law by Democratic President Joe Biden. The bill passed the House on a 225-201 vote, with 226 members voting by proxy. Friday’s ruling, powered by the 5th Circuit’s conservative majority, held that the proxy rule violated the U.S. Constitution’s quorum clause, which the court said requires a majority of House members to be physically present to pass legislation. “While the chambers of the legislature have much discretion regarding their rules of procedure, the Quorum Clause’s constraints on congressional power cannot be circumvented by congressional fiat,” wrote U.S. Circuit Judge Cory Wilson, an appointee of Republican President Donald Trump. While the decision concerns how the entire bill was passed, the relief that the 5th Circuit granted Paxton’s office was narrow, as it barred the U.S. Department of Justice and the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission from enforcing the pregnant workers provision against Texas. The DOJ, which defended the law, and Paxton’s office did not respond to requests for comment. U.S. Circuit Judge James Graves, an appointee of Democratic President Barack Obama, in a dissenting opinion called the ruling “illogical, inexplicable, and invalid.” He said the majority read a physical-presence requirement into the quorum clause that does not exist. Graves said the majority provided no explanation for why, if the entirety of the law was unconstitutionally passed, its ruling “should be limited only to one small sliver of the multitrillion dollar bill.”

items.title: Taylor Swift: 'Toy Story' song a welcome break from personal ballads | Philstar.com
items.excerpt: LOS ANGELES, United States — Taylor Swift, Oscar nominee? Penning a song for "Toy Story 5" offered the pop superstar the chance to write from a "fresh perspective" and pay homage to the animated film franchise she's loved since childhood. And "I Knew It, I Knew You" also could open the door for Swift to earn an Academy Award nod. "I'm loving, you know, writing from a fresh perspective," Swift told a recent press event. "Having a break from writing about my personal life is always kind of a relief." The 36-year-old released "I Knew It, I Knew You" in June, shortly before the premiere of "Toy Story 5." The country pop ballad touching on themes of friendship, nostalgia and reunions notched Swift two Grammy nominations including the coveted Song of the Year award, which she has never won. And it's considered a potential contender for Best Original Song at the Oscars. The track did lose this week at the Country Music Awards in the Single of the Year category to Ella Langley's ubiquitous "Choosin' Texas." Swift co-wrote her song with her frequent collaborator Jack Antonoff. It's inspired by Jessie, the animated cowgirl who in the franchise's fifth installment struggles to remain relevant in the face of a tablet's arrival.

items.title: Entertainment news roundup: 21 November 2026 | SVCZZ
items.excerpt: ## Leaving streaming The Resident left Netflix on Friday 20 November, with all six seasons leaving the service. The series stays available on Hulu in the US. ## Renewals, production and trailers Netflix confirmed Tokyo Swindlers season 2 on 20 November, with Go Ayano and Etsushi Toyokawa returning and Hitoshi One directing and writing. Filming is already under way, and a first-look image was released with the announcement. No release date has been announced; the confirmation follows an August report in Tokyo Sports of a quiet renewal. Season 3 of Cross has wrapped filming and is in post-production, creator Ben Watkins told ScreenRant in an interview published 18 November, with editing and scoring under way on the eight-episode season. No release date or premiere window has been announced. Sky and Peacock released the first teaser trailer for The Day of the Jackal season 2. Eddie Redmayne returns as the Jackal, and the season premieres in March 2027. First-look images were released for Grantchester series 11, the eleventh and final series. It airs in January 2027 on ITV and ITVX. ## Casting and new films Auli’i Cravalho has joined Milo Manheim, Whitney Peak and Stephen Kalyn in a new Serendipity film from Amazon MGM Studios and Miramax. Michael Showalter directs. The film updates the setting to the present day rather than rebooting the story. Variety reported the casting on 20 November, and no release date has been announced. Ahan Shetty has joined Vikram Bhatt’s 1920: Cold Winter, the sixth film in the 1920 horror franchise. Filming runs from December 2026 to March 2027 in Ooty and Mumbai. Pooja Sharma and Ashok Darji are to star in Nepali film Seto Coat, officially announced on 20 November. Filming begins on 25 November 2026. Advance booking opened for Paral Ko Aago ahead of its nationwide release on Friday 20 November, with over 100 shows secured. Suhana Thapa, Saugat Malla and Prakash Saput star in the film, inspired by a story by Guru Prasad Mainali. ## Box office Drishyam 3 has closed its theatrical run with Rs 594.89 crore worldwide and Rs 381.32 crore net in India, on a reported Rs 110 crore budget, a return of 246.65 percent. Koimoi ranks it the highest-grossing threequel. The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping took an estimated $51 million on Friday, including $21 million from Thursday previews. Deadline projects a $110 million domestic opening weekend. Final numbers are due on Monday. ## Deaths E.J. Carroll, the veteran character and voice actor known for The Deuce, Law & Order and Boardwalk Empire, has died aged 66. He died suddenly on Thursday 19 November on his way to a voiceover recording session. His manager confirmed the death to TheWrap, and no cause of death has been determined.
